newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia planning controls on Internet access.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia planning controls on Internet access.

text.p: Indonesia said on Wednesday it was planning to control access to the Internet as it goes ahead with its programme to build the infrastructure to make the information superhighway accessible to many of its 200 million citizens.

Minister for Tourism, Post and Telecommunications Joop Ave said in launching a new Internet service by partly state-owned telecommunications firm Indosat that it was a basic human right to have access to information.

But Ave later said Indonesia would not allow unrestricted growth of the Internet despite licensing a large number of local Internet Service Providers (ISPs) and a project to bring multimedia technology to the village level.
"We are very much for the free flow of information, but it is quite obvious that there are some limits," Ave told reporters.
"If we talk about pornography, we say no. If we talk about things that will hamper or threaten national security, we will say no," Ave said.
"The values of the nation will definitely have bearing upon the application of the Internet. We will not, for example, have 'anything goes'," he added.
Ave said he was not clear on the methods used by other countries in the region to restrict and control Internet access.
He said Indonesia would impose limitations in the future but the method had not yet been spelled out.
"I do think that we are planning that," Ave said.
Neighbouring Singapore licenses only three government-owned ISPs, compared with Indonesia's 42 mostly private ones. The computers of all three use proxy servers capable of blocking banned sites.
"I think the national values are important and if there is something against Indonesian national values, yes, we will block it," Ave said.

Craig Barrett, president of the world largest computer chip maker Intel Corporation, said in Jakarta on Tuesday he thought a figure of 200,000 Indonesians using the Internet by the year 2000 was "conservative".
Barrett referred to an industry survey as saying the number of Internet subscribers would exceed 50,000 in 1997 and increase at a rate of 70 percent per annum to more than 250,000 by 2001.
"If the number today is probably 50,000 and sales of computers are around 500,000 a year then it would not surprise me if it was not higher," he told a news conference.

Indosat (http://www.indosat.net.id) on Wednesday launched its new Indonesia Interactive service using Microsoft Corp software and Digital Equipment Corp hardware as a part of a new strategy to boost Internet commerce and use in Indonesia.
The service offers Jakarta Stock Exchange data, tourism information, real time flight information, entertainment, and Internet shopping in both English and Indonesian.
Speaking in a pre-recorded video message, Microsoft chairman Bill Gates said it was a visionary project to introduce new technology which would boost local content on the Internet.
"Today, the majority of the content on the Internet is English and is oriented around the United States, so it isn't always relevant for Indonesians," Gates said.
"Indonesia Interactive is a...platform for the creation of relevant content for Indonesians in their own language," he said.
